source_text: Hic nunc de fenore, cum interponit: et si feneraueritis a quibus speratis uos recepturos, quae gratia est uobis? percurre sequentia Ezechielis de eodem uiro iusto: pecuniam, inquit, suam fenore non dedet et quod abundauerit non sumet, fenoris scilicet redundantiam, quod est usura. prius igitur fuit, ut fructum fenoris eradicaret, quo facilius adsuefaceret hominem ipsi quoque fenori, si forte, perdendo, cuius fructum didicisset amittere. hanc etenim dicimus operam legis fuisse procurantis euangelio: quorundam tunc fidem paulatim ad perfectum disciplinae Christianae nitorem primis quibusque praeceptis balbutientis adhuc benignitatis informabat. nam et supra: et pignus, inquit, reddet debenti, — utique si non sit soluendo, quia solutori [utique] pignus restituendum esse utrum homo scriberet? — multo manifestius in Deuteronomio: non dormies super pignus eius, redditione reddes illi pallium circa solis occasum, et dormiet in pallio suo;
pass_a_gloss: Now he speaks about interest, when he interposes: and if you have lent to those from whom you hope to receive, what grace is to you? Run through the following of Ezekiel about the same just man: he says, he gave his money with interest, and what was abundant he did not take, clearly the excess of interest, which is usury. Therefore, it was first, that he might eradicate the fruit of interest, by which he might more easily accustom man to interest itself, if perhaps, by losing, he might learn to lose its fruit. We say this was the work of the law, which was preparing for the gospel: it was forming the faith of some, little by little, to the perfect discipline of Christian teaching, with the first and still stammering precepts of kindness. For also above: and he says, he will return the pledge to the debtor, — certainly if it is not to be paid, because the pledge is to be restored to the payer — much more clearly in Deuteronomy: he will not sleep upon his pledge, he will return the cloak to him at sunset, and he will sleep in his cloak; and he says, and the pledge he will return to the debtor, — certainly if it is not to be paid, because the pledge is to be restored to the payer, would a person write?

pass_b_english: Now, when it comes to interest, the question arises: if you lend to those you expect to get something back from, what's the point of being generous? Consider what Ezekiel says about a just man: he doesn't charge interest on his loans, and he doesn't take more than he's owed - in other words, he doesn't engage in usury. The idea was to eliminate the benefits of charging interest, making it easier for people to get used to the idea of lending without expecting something in return, perhaps by learning to lose the profits they once relied on. This, we argue, was the law's way of paving the way for the gospel: it was a gradual process of shaping people's faith, starting with basic, somewhat simplistic principles of kindness, to prepare them for the full discipline of Christian teaching. For instance, the law also says that a person should return a pledge to the debtor, especially if the debt can't be paid - after all, why would someone bother to write this down if it wasn't meant to be taken seriously? This is spelled out even more clearly in Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy), where it says that a person shouldn't keep someone's pledge overnight, but should return their cloak by sunset so they can sleep with some dignity (Ezekiel).

review.notes: Pass B contains significant errors in scripture attribution and content. It attributes the Deuteronomy passage to Ezekiel: '...return their cloak by sunset so they can sleep with some dignity (Ezekiel)'. It also misinterprets the Latin 'utique si non sit soluendo, quia solutori [utique] pignus restituendum esse utrum homo scriberet?' which is a rhetorical question about the necessity of writing down a debt if the pledge must be returned to the payer, whereas Pass B renders it as 'especially if the debt can't be paid - after all, why would someone bother to write this down if it wasn't meant to be taken seriously?'. Most critically, Pass B adds 'with some dignity' which is not in the Latin text.
reasons: Pass B incorrectly attributes the Deuteronomy quote to Ezekiel: '...return their cloak by sunset so they can sleep with some dignity (Ezekiel)'.
Pass B adds content not present in the Latin: 'with some dignity'.
